doc.title: Claude Williams interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Favorite experiences and admired saxophonists
summary: He enjoys differing musical ideas, admires Ben Webster and Hawkins, and recalls a 1976 Michael's Pub remark that his violin sounded like a horn.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Tell us, what is one of the most fun experiences you had as a musician, or one of the most awkward experiences?

Well I had a lot of fun because I played with a lot of different musicians and all of them, take three or four musicians, all of them play the same tune down, they all have different ideas. And one would be if it’s pretty to me it might not be pretty to you, but they play something else that’s pretty, it sounds pretty to you. And, oh I always enjoyed a saxophone. And you know I used to like the way Ben Webster would play you know, and some stuff Coleman Hawkins would play. So, when I came to New York, I was up in New York in ‘76 at a club they call the Michael’s Pub. And he said my violin sounded like an instrument, you know. Didn’t sound like you hear a violin in a symphony. Because I was playing changes and chords you know, the same as a sax. And like a trumpet or like, oh I heard, when Louis Armstrong played, he made an introduction to that song — I can’t think of that name, but he played a diminished chord for the introduction. [sings] Diminished. So I like those kinds of changes you know.
